titles.395: Annotatio II §.VII open: Nativitas of both Consubstantiations reborn — Lateran XIII under Innocent III
titles.396: Annotatio II §.VII: Lateran names Consubstantiation as already exploded — true accidents and true substance remain
titles.397: Annotatio II §.VII: Under remaining substances — BODY AND BLOOD; sense proves bread/wine, faith the rest
titles.398: Annotatio II §.VII close: After Berengar’s public censure; consub born from over-fighting him; stop before §.VIII

latin.395: §. VII. Ita habet Nativitas utriusque Consubstantiationis, Seculo 13, in Concilio Lateranensi, sub Innocentio III., rursus denatae, quod Concilium, Consubstantiationis, ceu jam tum explosæ & antiquatæ opinionis, mentionem, hisce injicit:
latin.396: Fuerunt, inquit, qui dicerent, quòd sicut post Consecrationem, vera panis remanent accidentia sic & vera panis substantia: quia sicut subjectum non potest subsistere sine Accidentibus, sic Accidentia non possunt subsistere sine subjecto.
latin.397: Sed panis & vini substantiis permanentibus ad prolationem illorum verborum CORPUS ET SANGUIS CHRISTI, veraciter incipiant esse SUB ILLIS (nempe sub panis & vini substantiis) ita quòd sub eisdem Accidentibus UTRUMQUE verè suscipitur PANIS ET CARO, VINUM ET SANGUIS, quorum alterum probat sensus, reliquum credit fides.
latin.398: Postquam jam tum Berengariana sententia, cui sese Consubstantiatores ex professo opposuerant, inque nimia ejus oppugnatione Consubstantiationem suam progenuerant, in ipsa Berengarii persona censuram publicam passa fuisset. Quo de in sequentibus Annotationibus commodior dicendi locus fuerit.

pass_a.395: §. VII. So stands the Nativity of either Consubstantiation, born again in the 13th Century in the Lateran Council under Innocent III — which Council injects mention of Consubstantiation as an opinion already then exploded and antiquated, in these words:
pass_a.396: There were, it says, who would say that just as after Consecration the true accidents of bread remain, so also the true substance of bread: because just as a subject cannot subsist without Accidents, so Accidents cannot subsist without a subject.
pass_a.397: But with the substances of bread and wine remaining, at the utterance of those words BODY AND BLOOD OF CHRIST, they truly begin to be UNDER THOSE (namely under the substances of bread and wine) so that under the same Accidents BOTH are truly received — BREAD AND FLESH, WINE AND BLOOD — of which the one sense proves, the rest faith believes.
pass_a.398: After the Berengarian sentence — to which the Consubstantiators had openly opposed themselves, and in excessive fighting of which they had begotten their Consubstantiation — had already then suffered public censure in Berengar’s own person. Of which there will be a more convenient place of speaking in the following Annotations.

395: §.VII: both Consubstantiations have their Nativity reborn in the 13th century — Lateran Council under Innocent III.
That council already treats Consubstantiation as an exploded, antiquated opinion, and names it thus:
396: Some said: after consecration, as true bread-accidents remain, so true bread-substance remains.
For a subject cannot stand without accidents, nor accidents without a subject.
397: With bread and wine substances still there, at Body and Blood of Christ those start to be under them.
Under the same accidents both are truly received — bread and flesh, wine and blood — sense proves one, faith the other.
398: By then Berengar’s sentence had already taken public censure in his person.
Consubstantiators had openly fought him — and in over-fighting him had begotten their own Consubstantiation.
More on that in the Annotations that follow.
Stop before §.VIII (PERDURATIO / revival after apparent extinction).

notes.398: Berengar censure; over-fight begets consub; stop §.VIII.
